utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, I gather you wish to raise something before we continue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. It concerns the testimony yesterday of Colonel Milovan Vlajkovic, and specifically matters that came up in the cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman and concerns what we regard as the improper use of Exhibit P1696 which was the RTS television report of a meeting of May 4th, 1999, attended by Mr. Milosevic and a number of other officials, some unnamed, but General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, General Lukic, and Mr. Milutinovic, and we're moving to strike that portion of the testimony, Your Honours, and I will now mention why. Mr. Ackerman quoted extensively from this television --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So starts on page 69, line 9 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we already have it updated so --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When roughly was it in the course of the day, two-thirds of the way through or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah, roughly, I would say that would be about right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 3D, sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The exhibit is P1696, and that's the R -- the RTS television report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know if it was in the last session, 16.080. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And Mr. Ackerman quoted extensively from this P1696 and he said, among other things, the security forces dealt with numerous cases of violence, I'm going to paraphrase here, killings, pillage and other crimes. The state authorities legally and in an unbiased manner carried out their duties, it was concluded that these measures had made such actions impossible and it went on to say military courts acting in accordance with the proceedings envisaged in war conditions have already passed a large number of sentences ranging from five to 20 years' imprisonment for the crimes committed. Now, Mr. Ackerman apparently assumed the truth of what was contained in this article and said to the witness on cross-examination why didn't General Ojdanic pass this on to the collegium. We say this was improper for several reasons. First, P1696 at that point in the case had not been admitted into evidence as an exhibit. It's ironic to note that Mr. Ackerman in his Pavkovic response to the OTP's second request for admission of exhibits from the bar table objected to a proposed OTP exhibit which was a newspaper article, and in his objection noted: "OTP P1010 is an inadmissible newspaper article. The Trial Chamber has held that newspaper articles are inadmissible and unreliable." And Mr. Ackerman in making that statement correctly referred to transcript 8561, 8562 of the record. And at that time, Your Honour, this was on January 17th, 2007, Mr. Cepic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, there's a difference between what Mr. Ackerman may assert as a question and what the evidence in this case is. Now, this witness yesterday made it clear that he knew nothing about any of this, and it doesn't amount to any evidence in this case at this stage. We have a rather different approach from perhaps what has always been traditional in this institution of seeing that there can be value in a document to understand the answer to the question without necessarily treating the document as having any probative value in itself. This is one of these examples. We've made it clear what we think of reports of newspaper or television or radio but it doesn't mean it can't be a foundation for a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But the document, Your Honour, has no relevance unless we assume the truth of what was in it because he asked the witness, Mr. Ackerman asked the witness why didn't General Ojdanic pass this information on to the collegium, and we're going to show by evidence in this case that the reason he didn't pass this on to the collegium is that most of those evidence in -- most of those statements in that report were false --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer to the question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- and misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the answer to the question is do you know why it was? No, I don't. End of story.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But it assumes the truth of what is in the article as if General Ojdanic did something improper and we shouldn't have to rebut that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not part of the evidence in this case unless someone has agreed with it. On what basis -- bearing in mind all we've said so far, could you regard that as positive evidence of the facts set out in the article?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, I certainly don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can't if you follow the rules we've been following.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So is it my understanding, Your Honour -- maybe I've misunderstood. Is it my understanding that this exhibit will have no weight whatsoever in your consideration of this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm about to ask Mr. Ackerman for his comment, but on the face of it unless -- you've told me it hasn't been admitted, it's been used only for this purpose, the answer to the question was no, I don't and therefore there appears to be no positive evidence emanating from the use of this article at this stage in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Nor do I think that Your Honour should give any weight whatsoever to the answer of Colonel Vlajkovic that this was not -- that General Ojdanic didn't somehow turn over this information which we regard as false to the collegium. That should also be stricken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that's what he said. He said that there were no reports at -- referred to in the minutes and briefings until early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The question was, Your Honour: "And you know, didn't you," this is Mr. Ackerman. "And you knew, didn't you, that there was an important issue that was being discussed in the western press and an issue was being made about it. My question to you that you didn't answer is: Do you know why General Ojdanic failed to take steps to deal with that," in other words, assuming the truth of what was in the article, do you know why he failed to take steps to deal with that and failed to report it to the collegium, a grossly unfair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, two things: The witness's answer does not assume the truth of the question -- the events referred to in the question; and secondly, you should have objected at the time if that was your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That was my position -- let me tell you why I didn't object, Your Honour. I didn't object for a few reasons. One is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do we need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I want to explain that for the record. You asked me, Your Honour, and I want to explain for the record why I didn't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know you're using your own valuable time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think it's important, Your Honour. We'll take our chances on that. And I didn't object because for one thing, I didn't even know about this article until Mr. Ackerman brought it pup. And the second thing, I just assumed -- Mr. Ackerman is a respected colleague and I don't like to interfere with a respected colleague if he regards this as essential for his case. Frankly, we should have objected, but I go on the theory, Your Honour, it's never too late to do the right thing and I'm objecting now while Mr. -- while Colonel Vlajkovic is still here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The respected ones, Mr. Sepenuk, are usually -- are the ones most likely to be pushing the boundaries. They know that their job is to push the boundaries as far as they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I don't like to assume that about my fellow counsel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Some would say --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Some might say they aren't doing their duty unless they do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, we could probably spend a long time talking about that, Your Honour. Anyway, that's my position. I think the exhibit should be given no weight whatsoever. I think that Colonel Vlajkovic's testimony regarding this exhibit should be stricken and not considered by the Court for anything. We don't know who gave the information in this statement, by the way, the only one quoted in this article is President Milosevic toward the end. We got this article -- this source from the government. It says: "Government control station under tight control of the Milosevic regime." This might have been a bit of wartime propaganda here and there's been no evidence whatsoever tying General Ojdanic or, for that matter, any of these other defendants who are mentioned to the specifics of that article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, do you wish to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour. The proposition that it wasn't known about until I brought it up is not exactly -- shouldn't be exactly correct since it was sent to everybody at the beginning of the direct examination of this witness that I was going to use it during cross-examination. So if they didn't know, they should have known. The second thing is that the content of that particular document is also repeated in Politika and in a video V0001824/1A, both of which could be made available if necessary. And there may be additional evidence. The other thing that I think is very important to consider is that this document was used simply as a foundational document for a -- the basis for asking the question in the first place, and that was its only use at that point. Now, it may be that there is evidence that could be put on to actually prove that meeting and its contents but that remains to be seen. The other thing is that it was a double-headed question, as you might recall. I wasn't talking just about the May 4th meeting, but also talking about the meetings of the 16th and 17th of May, and I think those are proven without any doubt in this case now that General Ojdanic became aware by the 16th or the 17th of May. So my question about why it wasn't brought up in the collegium, those issues brought up in the collegium until some time in early June I think still may have some validity, although I didn't ever see that as a major part of my cross-examination in the first place. There may be a very good reason why it wasn't brought up. But in any event, I think -- I strongly oppose the motion of Mr. Sepenuk that that testimony be stricken from the record. I don't think it should be. I don't think it was improper or anything I did was improper. So that's my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We appreciate that the way we've treated exhibits can give rise to misunderstandings and we regret that, but for the avoidance of doubt, let me repeat that this is an entirely procedural issue. It has no bearing on the evaluation of the probative value of documents. We believe that to fully understand the evidence you need to have available to you as part of the record the material that was used for the purpose of posing the questions. However, as I've just explained, that does not make this document, P1696, evidence of the truth of its contents in this context because the witness denied any knowledge of it, as we read his answers. It doesn't follow that newspaper articles may have absolutely no probative value at all. For example, we found assistance from newspaper articles in deciding whether or not to admit press statements sought by the first accused. Now, you can understand why trying to find out whether or not it appeared in the press is relevant to determining whether we should admit it. It's quite another matter, however, to decide what is the probative value of the press statement. These are complex issues that the Trial Chamber will have to deal with when it comes to deliberate on all the evidence in the case. So the normal rules that you understand, Mr. Sepenuk, about relevance and probative value do apply here, but you should not assume that because a document gets on to our record to reflect the questions put that we will give it a weight that will not be appropriate on the basis of the normal rules of relevancy and probative value. So we actually welcome the intervention to try to give clarification to this, but we do not think the appropriate course is to strike it from the record. It may be that other evidence will materialise in due course on which this does have a bearing, and we would have to look at the evidence in its entirety to decide what to do and you will have -- clearly have an opportunity to address us on that in your final submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. And just for the sake of the record, I want to stress that I don't think this exhibit should be given any weight whatsoever and there will be testimony in the case to show that a good portion of what is in this article is false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But let's assume we hear from the editor of RTS about the way in which this article was compiled and presented and bearing in mind the rules of hearsay evidence, the position would change and the record should be there to reflect what happened earlier in the case. So we hear what you say, we hear your position, we note it, we think it hasn't been prejudiced at this stage by the evidence that has been given so far by this witness. And therefore, you need not fear that we will be holding against you the truth of the contents of this article -- or these articles at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We can proceed now, Mr. Visnjic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- can we. Let's have the witness. You'll see why I like to get witnesses finished the day they first appear here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vlajkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your re-examination by Mr. Visnjic will continue in a moment. It is important for you to bear in mind that the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your evidence to speak the truth continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit 3D1109, pages 2 and 3 at the same time on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, yesterday Mr. Ackerman suggested a few things to you in respect of which he said that they could have led to a mistake when making entries in the register. I will go through each and everything that Mr. Ackerman suggested to you, so we will have a look as to what this really was like. The first thing that Mr. Ackerman suggested to you was that perhaps the document on the resubordination of the command of the 3rd Army, that is under entry 248, was supposed to be attached to the document in 247, another document of the 3rd Army that was registered under number 872-137/1. Now I would like to ask you to look at column 7 on page 3 of this document; and if possible, could you please read out for us what the content of this order is, the one registered in 247.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The content of the order is: "Report on rejecting order by soldier from the 3rd Company or the 3rd Battalion of the 125th Motorised Brigade in the zone of responsibility of the Pristina Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In view of the heading of this document - we don't have the document before us right now - in this document 3D1106, on resubordination on the basis of your knowledge, should these two documents have been entered in the same rubric 247?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the content of the document, it can be concluded that they are not directly related, one did not produce the other and therefore they cannot be registered under the same number, they are not registered under the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next thing that -- the next suggestion that Mr. Ackerman made to you was that numbers 247 and 248 should be in the same archive list; that is to say, 3D1108, that is the archive list, rather, number 21606. Yesterday you went together with him through archive list 21606, that which is 3D1108, and you established that this number, 247, is not on that archive list. I would like to ask you to have a look at this. You still have page 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just leave third page of D1109, 3D. [Interpretation] Could we also enlarge column 10, that is to say the upper left-hand corner, a bit more, further down, please. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, now I would like to ask you to tell us in which archive list is the document from column 247?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is in archive list number 1548 dash, if I see this right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the document from column 248, in which archive list is that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in archive list 21606.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, does that mean that these two documents cannot be in the same archive list by any means, 21606, 3D1108, as was suggested to you yesterday by Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this, it is obvious that these are two archive lists where these documents were registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So there wasn't any need for us to look for it in 3D1108?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't any need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P1459.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if you remember, yesterday Mr. Ackerman also suggested to you that numbers 72 that are in the upper right-hand corner and 81/3 in the middle of this document are in actual fact proof of this document having been registered in one of the registers or log-books; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now display on e-court Defence Exhibit 6D1130, page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That is a survey of the archive material of the Army of Yugoslavia 1998/1999, and on this first page there is an entry that says 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 49 of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you see column 72?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the document referred to in this column, is that the document that you saw a few moments ago, P1459, the document of the 3rd Army on resubordination?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The filing number and column 7 where the content of the document is registered, well. That is that document..

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at column 10.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In column 10 there is number 81/3, that is precisely the same document that we saw on P1459.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us have a look at page 2. Who actually produced this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please say what it says in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia chief, strictly confidential, number 1737-4, the 31st of October, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, who was the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2001 the Chief of General Staff was General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, and this information is for the OTP, this is a list of documents that General Pavkovic handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor in July 2002. This list is practically, or rather, the -- these numbers are practically from the list of documents that were handed over to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to look at page 53 of this same document, column 102.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If you look at this document under number 102, it is a report of the 3rd Army, strictly confidential, number 872-137/1, and this is in actual fact the document that we saw a few moments ago in 3D1109 in column 247. Colonel, what we have here is a rather more detailed description of the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extraordinary report to the Supreme Command Staff on the fact that the 3rd Company of the 3rd/125th Motorised Brigade, about 80 soldiers, refused obedience in the broader area of Kosare, detailed report on two pages compiled by the commander of the 3rd Army personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, now I'm asking you again on the basis of this more detailed description of the document in column 102 which I would like to note is in column 247 of 3D1109. Would the document on the resubordination of the 3rd Army have to be registered in the same column as the document that you quoted just now?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 3D145. While we're still at this exhibit, Your Honour, I would just like to draw your attention to something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several hundred, or rather, several hundred documents that are referred to in document 3D1106, not a single document was registered, for example, as 872 and then, say, number 24, and then slash and then, say, number 3. There is no document of this kind except for this document, 1459, that has also -1, 2, or 3, as is the case with this document, P1459 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a minute. Your question on the last exhibit was translated: "Now I'm asking you again on the basis of this more detailed description of the document in column 102 ... would the document on the resubordination of the 3rd Army have to be registered in the same column as the document that you quoted just now?" Now, is that the question you wanted to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and the witness said no, as far as I can remember. No, no, it's the document on resubordination from the 3rd Army, produced by the 3rd Army, not resubordination of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you're understanding me clearly, and it may be a translation question. Let me read the question again: "Would the document have to be registered in the same column?"

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The question should be: Should the document be registered in the same column if they have a common content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's as far as you want to go, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, would you like to ask that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So, Colonel, you had before you two documents of the 3rd Army, one is the document that you quoted from column 102 and that is the special report to the Supreme Command Staff on the refusal of obedience of a particular soldier and so on and so forth; and the second document was one that pertained to a report of the commander of the 3rd Army on the non-execution of an order of commands and units of the MUP for resubordination. On the basis of what you know, could these two documents be registered in the same column or should they be registered in the same column?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules on office work, they could not and should not be registered in the same column because in terms of their content they are not directly related to one another. One did not stem from the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have 4D135 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you are familiar with this document. You were examined on it yesterday by Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Stamp, too. Mr. Ackerman put it to you that there is no basis for a document on the resubordination, that's P1459, to be part of this analysis; and on the other hand, Mr. Stamp put it to you that on the last page of this document there are reasons why this document should be part of this analysis. And in the final answer you said that, in fact, the team leader working on this report would be the one to make the final decision as to why this document was not made part of this analysis. Could you please tell us, on the basis of this document that you see in front of you, could you identify the team leader or where this analysis was done at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what we can see from the document, the analysis was done in the operations and staff affairs sector, to be quite specific as to the team leader who did this analysis, I couldn't really tell you that because this is not seen from this document, I mean the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, let me ask you something. Do you rule out the possibility that the reason why this document was not made part of this analysis is precisely the fact that this document never reached the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN VLAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it never reached it, then it could not be subject of an analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This completes my examination of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vlajkovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to assist us. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, can you indicate what your plans are for the rest of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Radoicic should take between half an hour and 45 minutes; witness Uzelac 20 minutes; witness Pantelic, well, let's say up to half an hour, not more, I'm being optimistic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about Gojovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've already sent Gojovic home. There was no way we could have examined him. We will bring him back after the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean before the adjournment. I said "after," but I meant his break, Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have Mr. Radoicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: My name is Milan Radoicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you on the 17th of August, 2007, give a statement to the investigators of the Defence team of General Ojdanic and did you sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you came to The Hague were you able to go through this statement; and if you were to give evidence before this Court, would you have given the same answers to the questions that you did in that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes, entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Defence Exhibit 3D1108 -- no, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 1111 perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 1111. Could the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit 3D1108.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recognise this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is this document? Who produced it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: This document was produced immediately after the end of the aggression on the orders of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff. It quite specifically regulates the procedure for the archiving of all of the documents produced in the period from the beginning until the end of the aggression, and this order regulates the procedure to be applied by all the organizational units of the Supreme Command Staff as it was at the time, including all the elements that pertained to the chef de cabinet of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff. This list that is here in front of me, or rather, this page is part of this procedure that was carried out in the office of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood it correctly from previous evidence, such lists were then taken to the military archive together with all the documents, relevant documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to the order that I mentioned, the procedure that was to be followed by all the organizational units of the Supreme Command Staff was regulated in great detail, gathering of the documents, processing of the documents in the manner that is prescribed by the regulations in force at the time on the work of the military archive and of all those who had the obligation to submit or to take out certain documents from the military archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us where was this form filled in, because I can see that some items were typed in.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not only the organizational units of the Supreme Command Staff that were under the obligation to comply with the procedure relating to the documents. The military archive itself was under the obligation to carry out certain procedures. They had certain forms and certain procedures that were binding on all of the parties handing in documents, and this list is one such document. It stipulates what and how is to be handed over to the military archive. It was impossible to hand over a single document outside of this procedure because the responsible officials from the military archive were not allowed and did not want to receive any documents if they did not comply with the procedure for the archiving of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I asked you where those forms were filled in.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: The military archive filled it in, and they were submitted by those who submitted documents. The office of the Supreme Command Staff chief was under the obligation to fill in this empty form in the prescribed manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two answers there, Mr. Visnjic. It says the military archive filled it in, and then it says the office of the Supreme Command Staff chief was under the obligation to fill in this empty form. So who did it? I don't know at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let us clear this up. Who filled in the empty form?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, in this specific case it was the office of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, once a form that has been filled in comes into the archive with the documents, do you know what the procedure was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: The responsible person from the military archive received the documents in the same order as listed here one document after the other. So the responsible person handed in the document, in this case it was the responsible person from the office, and on the other hand it was taken receipt of by the responsible person from the military archive. And if the document had everything it had to contain, then it could be received. If it didn't meet those requirements, it was not received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could we scroll down this last page a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope you got that message, Mr. Visnjic, to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, who signed this document on the right-hand side, the signature there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: At the very outset I said that the procedure of preparing and handing over the entire documentation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Simple question. Please listen carefully to the question, which is: "Who signed the document on the right side?" That's a very easy one to answer if you can read the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just had the intention of explaining this here, the first name and the last name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If Mr. Visnjic wants an explanation, he'll ask for it. Just tell us who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I signed the document, as authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, on the right-hand side, the handwritten text and the signature, who signed that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Column 7, towards the bottom, vertically written text and there is a signature.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Could it please be turned around and zoomed in because, quite simply, I cannot see who wrote that and signed that. This is the first time I see it this way. It says: "Received for the military archives by warrant officer first class Dusan Mladenovic." And it's probably the signature of the authorised official from the military archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to move on to another exhibit now, 3D1078.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, General Ojdanic in March 2002 sent you a letter. At that time you were working in the Ministry of Defence, the Federal Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At that time you and General Ojdanic were not on the best of terms personally; I see that from the content of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't put it that way, that we weren't on the best of terms; quite simply, there wasn't a quality communication, which does not mean that we were not on the best of terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to read out paragraph 3 to you. Paragraph 3 of this letter that says: "To my astonishment on the 21st of February, 2002, in the newspaper Vojska," army, "on pages 8 and 9 a text appeared 'problems with resubordination of MUP forces.' One of the documents under the subheading the 'summarization of report results' is something I'm seeing for the first time a report of the command of the 3rd Army, strictly confidential number 872-94/1-2 about the resubordination of units and organs of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia." Colonel, can you tell me what it was that General Ojdanic asked you to do in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: He asked me through this letter to provide an answer as to whether I'm aware of such a document; and if so, whether such a document ever reached the office, the cabinet, of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 2 of this document, also paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph General Ojdanic writes to you and says: "As Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, I want my conscience to be perfectly clear from every point of view. You know full well -- you know full well what my conscience and responsibility are in carrying out my functional duty. Can you imagine that had I received such a report I would have silently passed over it without having directly informed my collegium and Supreme Command about it, examined the proposed measures, and notified the command of the 3rd Army of all this as per the methodology of work which was applied by the Supreme Command Staff?" Colonel, you worked with General Ojdanic for a long time. How long?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: From the end of 1993 when he was appointed commander of the 1st Army up until the end of 1996/beginning of 1997, when General Ojdanic was transferred to become deputy Chief of General Staff. It was the end of 1998 when he was appointed Chief of General Staff. I was asked to assume the duty of the deputy chef de cabinet to the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Do I respond to this and does it suit me to assume that duty --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not deal with it so extensively. You've known him for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Almost ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the basis of everything that you know about General Ojdanic, what General Ojdanic wrote here, is that correct? Is that the way he reacts when he receives a report that has the kind of content that this document to the 3rd Army had?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I fully accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Visnjic, what kind of a question is that? If you've got a particular incident to put to the witness that he can help us with or ask him about specific occasions, fine, but to put a question about a similar set of circumstances to this in general is not going to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to move on to the next exhibit, 3D1077.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, a few days later you replied to General Ojdanic by way of this letter. In paragraph 3 of this document that is going to appear before you right now, what did you actually establish in relation to this document of the 3rd Army that General Ojdanic asked you about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely this, what I wrote here; that is to say that I did not have any knowledge about that report and since at that time I was already working at the Ministry of Defence, it's -- it was almost two years from that period, if I can put it that way. I checked with my colleagues who had stayed at the office of the Chief of General Staff, and I was given this kind of return information, as I wrote here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. I'd like to ask you a few questions. Let me follow up with that letter, Exhibit 3D1078. It's my understanding that this is a letter from General Ojdanic to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: If it's the letter that I do not find here, it's not visible on my screen -- ah, yes. If it's this letter, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the bottom of page 1 of the English and I believe it may be the very top of page 2 in the B/C/S he indicates that he's asked you to help him locate this document. And he says: "Unfortunately you turned a deaf ear to my request for reasons and intentions known to you." Did you respond to this letter, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I don't understand, what question are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, he seems to be indicating that he had made an earlier request for the archive list and the combat documentation. And he says: "Unfortunately you turned a deaf ear to my request for reasons and intentions known to you." And then he goes on to say: "It is hypocritical, to say the least, to refer to the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council which allegedly prevents you from fulfilling my request because I am seeking a strictly confidential combat document which was published publicly in the Vojska magazine." So is that correct, had he previously asked you for this document or information about the archive list concerning this document and you had turned him down?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: The overall communication between General Ojdanic and me personally was not regulated by way of particular correspondence. This is the only correspondence we had, which means that before that and after that, our communication was regulated, as was fitting in terms of the relationship that he and I had. He made a request, either orally or on a little piece of paper through one of his associates. Now, why I did not answer, I cannot say now quite precisely. The only thing I can do is assume that in this period in between, a decision had been made by the Supreme Defence Council that had given a certain number of protective measures in terms of treating documents that are marked as a state secret, military secret, strictly confidential, and so on. So with these documents one had to behave only in the prescribed way. If it is necessary for me to describe this prescribed way to you, I stand ready to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: I'm not clear about your answer. Are -- did you reply to this request from General Ojdanic; and if so, was that by a written communication or by letter or by telephone call or in person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, I think -- well, that is to say that I cannot remember with certainty now, but as for one of the persons who had direct cooperation with him, I gave a response orally that I could not seek that document except in the prescribed manner, but I did reply. And I assume that this letter is precisely a response indicating his justified dissatisfaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: His justified dissatisfaction with your first reply, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I also have a question, then did you respond to this letter from I think it's the 2nd of March, did you respond to this letter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely. The letter I have before me now on the monitor caused the official written response, the one that was displayed on the screen previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me then go back to your -- your statement which is Exhibit 3D1111. If I understand it correctly, your job during 1999 and during the NATO air-strikes, did you work for Colonel Vlajkovic? Was he your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I worked with Colonel Vlajkovic. I did not work for him. I worked for the cabinet of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, or rather, the Supreme Command Staff. I was officially his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were officially Colonel Vlajkovic's deputy, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us which meetings you attended. Did you attend the meetings that we've been referring to here as the daily evening briefings during -- during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: During the war at all sessions of the collegium of the Supreme Command Staff, Colonel Vlajkovic was present. I think that once or twice in a period of time while he was absent - this was justified absence - I attended these sessions once or twice, not more than that. As for all the other 70 days out of the total of 72, Colonel Vlajkovic was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I need some clarification about this. We have some minutes from meetings that were referred to as the VJ collegium, and some witnesses have referred to these daily evening briefings as collegium meetings and I think sometimes as meetings of the Supreme Command Staff. Is there any difference between all that? Can you explain? Because the only document that I've seen that's described as a meeting of the VJ collegium during the 78 days of the NATO air-strikes is from the 9th of April.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I cannot judge about somebody's precise or imprecise wording, whether somebody called it meetings or sessions, but the official terminology that is recorded in all the written and unwritten documents, this body is called the collegium and its meetings are called sessions of the collegium of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. They were held every day in the evening, as I assume you have known for a while now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any difference then in the personnel who are members of what's called the Supreme Command Staff and what you referred to just now as the collegium? Are we talking about the same people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: The regular composition of the collegium meant that body, and perhaps sometimes there was a need for the part of that composition to attend for a meeting to be held in a broader or a narrower composition, but officially that was the collegium of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if someone talks about the Supreme Command Staff, does that mean the same thing as the collegium or are there some additional people on the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, in the regular conceptual formulation of this body, that was the staff or the collegium of the staff of the Supreme Command, that would be more or less the same thing. But based on the assessment of the superior commander, that would be the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, that body could in the formal number that was -- that there could be more people or less people, and in some cases the collegium session would be held in the extended composition. That was up to the assessment of the chief of the Supreme Command, both at the time when it was the Supreme Command and in the period immediately before the aggression and after the aggression. So it depended on the actual need and the assessment of the Chief of the General Staff or of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff. That body could either have the composition as provided for in the organizational chart or could be narrower or extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was it General Ojdanic as the chief who made that decision about whether it was narrower or extended?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in your statement where you describe the duties of your office, in paragraph 3 you mentioned that it included preparing all or almost all documents being sent to the military office of the president of the FRY. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that correct, it was the duty of the office you worked in to prepare all or almost all documents being sent to the military office of Mr. Milosevic, the president of the FRY? It's not the only thing you did, but that was one of the duties of your office, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so, but the stress is here on the preparation of all or almost all. This doesn't mean that the cabinet was the only body that prepared all of the documents, but it was responsible for preparing all documents, either processed in the cabinet or in the organizational elements of the supreme -- of the staff or of subordinate commands, but it was responsible for preparing and processing all the documents in the manner that I described in my previous answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, can you help us. Can you tell us what exactly was the military office of President Milosevic? How many people were in that? What did they do? Were they civilians or military persons? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I was never in a position to see the organizational chart and the establishment of the structure of the cabinet of the military office of the president, in other words, but my communication with the military office of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia went through the chef de cabinet of the military office of the president of the FRY or his deputy or any responsible person that was in charge of a task or the kind of job that we were supposed to do together that I was in contact with, including the secretary of the chief of the military office of the president of the FRY. I had no reason to make this communication broader or deeper, so I have no knowledge apart from what I just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the exhibits we have in this case is P2166, which is about a meeting of the Inter-Departmental Staff for Suppression of Terrorism, and the person listed as taking the minutes in that meeting is Lieutenant-General Slavoljub Susic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I knew him to the extent that allowed -- that our official relationship allowed, not more, not less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was he a member of the military department of President Milosevic or the military office of President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, his function was chief of the military office of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He was not part of it. He was, quite literally, the most responsible person and the highest-ranking officer in the military office of the president of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know the name of his deputy?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the actual period. In the period when the Supreme Command Staff operated, I had no opportunity to find out or to see any other person apart from his secretary, who was also his deputy. But in the period before the aggression, and I can't really now tell you whether it was also after the aggression, but before the aggression I was communicating with his deputy, at that time it was Colonel Nedjo Danilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to talk about the -- the archive list that Mr. Visnjic asked you about. I think that's Exhibit P -- or 3D1108. And if first we could go to page 1 of that document in both languages. Colonel, in the upper left-hand corner there's a stamp which is translated in English as "Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Supreme Command Staff, cabinet of the chief." It has a number and is dated the 10th of August, 1999. Now, do I understand correctly, did you in your office prepare this list, this typewritten list?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we're looking at the same document, but the date is not here, the date as far as I can see it, it's not really all that legible, it's the 16th of June, 1999. I don't know if we're talking about the same document, and if we're talking about the upper left-hand corner there, there was the stamp of the relevant organizational unit of the Supreme Command Staff, in this case it was the cabinet of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff and the right and the obligation to use this stamp and to apply to the documents as prescribed, that all the elements of the Army of Yugoslavia were under the obligation to apply their stamps. I can see this document here, it is hardly legible, but I think it is a confidential document. I can't see the number, it's -- it says here "confidential." But I think that the date is the 16th of June, 1999, if we're talking about the same document, it's not 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if I -- you heard "1992" I misspoke or was mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on that seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the English it's been translated as being 10 August 1999. It may not be very legible. We've tried to make it a little bigger. I don't know if that helps you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is the case, indeed. Yes, it's the 10th, although again I can't really see it here, whether it's the 10th or the 16th zoomed in as it is. It is number 8 and the -- it is 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: So it's a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could zoom out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I got the answer to my original question. Was this list prepared by you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, in -- by reply to a question by the Defence counsel, I spoke about that and I will repeat the same answer to you. The form was obtained from the military archive, it was an empty form --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We got --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- with all the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We got all that. We know there were spaces and they had to be filled in. The question is: Did you fill them in, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean I personally or we as the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: First of all, you personally.

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't do that job, but I was responsible to the chef de cabinet and to the chief of the Supreme Command for the proper performance of this job, but the technical preparation and the actual typing in of all this information into this form, this was done by the responsible persons, including the chief of the office of the cabinet of the Supreme Command Staff. So that was an organizational unit within the cabinet of the Supreme Command Staff or chief of the Supreme Command Staff or the General Staff chief, they had to treat all the documents in accordance with the relevant regulations in force in a proper and responsible manner, including in the period of time when the Supreme Command Staff was activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So the actual filling in of the blank form was done by personnel in your office. Was that people under either your control or the control of Colonel Vlajkovic; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The stamp in the upper left-hand corner where we decided the date was from August 1999, who put that stamp on this document? Was that done in your office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. The stamp and all the other -- this stamp and all the other stamps were kept and used in that room in that organizational unit which was called the office of the cabinet, so they had a right to use it and also the responsibility for the proper use of the stamps and seals of the cabinet of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff and the chief of the General Staff and the chief of the Supreme Command Staff and the Chief of the General Staff, so both the cabinet and the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. When you say "they," isn't this your office? Shouldn't you be saying "we"? Didn't you also have authority to use that stamp?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, I just gave you a quite specific answer to your question when you asked me who did that, and I can just as well say "we."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know in particular whose job it would have been to put the stamp and the dates and the number on this particular document? Was there one person whose job it was to do that kind of thing or did that duty rotate depending on the kind of situation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, on some occasions it changed according to the planned schedule, but to be quite specific it was the chief of the office of the chief of the cabinet of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, at that time it was the warrant officer first class Milorad Jankovic. And from the handwriting used for the numbers and the designation of the degree of classification, I can recognise his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, on the right side of this document at the top there's another stamp which has an inventory number and a date of 24 September 1999 and a number of documents and a number of pages. Now, am I correct in understanding that's a stamp that must have been put on in the archives -- or at least not in your office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether you've encountered anything of the sort before, but this is not a stamp. These are all the same rubrics that are usually present here in the upper right-hand corner, this is not a stamp, this is not a seal. This is simply a box in the form where you could put in the register number, the date, and everything else that is in here. So the inventory number was not put in in the cabinet, it was put in in the archive during the handover procedure. So on the left-hand side you have the stamp of the party handing the document over, and in the right-hand side there was a space for the responsible person in the military archive to supply the proper inventory number to indicate the date when this was done, and also to indicate the number of documents that were handed over. So this is not a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I -- I understand now that this is part of the blank form, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the number of documents and number of pages that are filled in in handwriting there, where would that have been done? Would that have been done in your office before the documents were shipped out or would it have been done at the archives when they received it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Right at the beginning in the order of the chief of the Supreme Command, as I stressed, everything was regulated in greatest detail. The military archive did not have the personnel, the material or other capabilities to send its staff from one organizational unit to the other so that -- there were several reasons why they couldn't do that. It was the obligation on the part of us who were handing in the documents to take it to the military archive and to carry out this handover of the documents, the take-over of documents, whatever you like to call it, in the premises of the military archive, that's where it was done, in the military archive, the handover between the official in the relevant organizational unit of the General Staff and the responsible person representing the military archive of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need a little more time. Can we take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can, yeah. Mr. Radoicic, we have to have a break at this stage, that will be for 20 minutes. Could you leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you again at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, if you can just be patient with me a little longer, I want to walk through the process to the end. So once this form is filled out in your office, I take it that these documents that are going into the archives are placed in some kind of box or container to physically be delivered to the archives, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: We, quite literally, had courier bags, that is what they were called. In terms of their size they're very big bags, documentation could fit into it to the extent which it was needed at the time for several reasons. These bags even had a special place for a padlock in order to secure everything that was contained in the bag until it was handed over. On that occasion it is precisely these courier bags that were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know how the courier bags then are taken from your office and delivered to archives? Who does that or who did that at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: That is to say that in this concrete case this was done by the head of the office together with his deputy. I don't know to what extent you understand the idea of an office. It is not an office in the sense of a physical room, it is simply a word that is used. So this office had log-books and personnel and technical facilities, including operators. Specifically, this was done by the head of office and his deputy. By taking this bag, including its content, leaving the premises of the cabinet, going to the vehicle involved, because at that point in time the military archives were at a location that was a few kilometres away from the location where the cabinet of the Chief of General Staff was of the Army of Yugoslavia, specifically from the street of Neznanog Junaka to Bircaninova where the premises of the Ministry of Defence are now. In the basement even before the aggression, the military archives were located there; that is to say from the cabinet premises to the vehicle, from the vehicle to the location where the military archives were, and then from the vehicle entering the military archives and in -- on the premises of the military archives there was this procedure of handover that took several days in terms of time because this is a very delicate and responsible job to look at each and every document. That would be it in the briefest possible terms. If there's anything else in connection with the procedure and everything that has to be done or was envisaged in that procedure or that was to be expected, I can speak about it in greater detail, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I do have a couple more questions. From your answer then, so it's delivered in the courier bags by personnel from your office, and at the archives you told me the procedure sometimes could take days to actually get those documents logged in at the archives; is that correct? Because you're going through the list and pulling out each document one by one and making sure that the number of documents and the number of pages as listed are correct. Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Precisely. The procedure of the handover in terms of the people who did not have occasion to work on this or see this seems simply; however, as you said this now this is exceptionally responsible and very complex because the responsible person from the military archives was duty-bound to carry out a full examination, not a partial one, a full examination of everything that he was receiving. These documents had to be either originals or, if so prescribed, there had to be a second and a third copy, also originals. There were few occasions when only copies of documents would be received. As you said a few moments ago, in particular, the number of pages, whether the first page is one that matches all the attachments and so on. It's a very delicate job. And finally, if the document contains several pages, several attachments, was it complete, was it properly filed, was it properly bound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think -- I think I heard it from Colonel Vlajkovic that at the archives there was -- there was one person who would be responsible for receiving all the documents that were on this list; in other words, the job wasn't divided up among several persons. There was just a single individual who would be responsible in this case for dealing with this list of some 110 archive units or archive items. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be quite sure that that is the way it was, as my colleague Mr. Vlajkovic said to you. But I know in terms of this entire work on behalf of the cabinet of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, the General Staff, on behalf of the archives, the head of the archives, they would have to assess in terms of the number of the documents, the complexity of these documents whether it was necessary to engage one or two persons. On specific occasions, I did not attend the handover, I just got a feedback, or rather, a report from the person who carried this out, and then I informed the chef de cabinet about that. I did not -- I do not recall having informed him of the number of persons who took part in this from the military archives. Was it the chief of the military archives who assessed that the documents coming from the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command or from some other organic entity of the Supreme Command Staff required two or three or more persons? I really could not have that particular information. But at any rate, the procedure involving the signing and the receipt, or rather, the handover, all this was signed by one person, one person on behalf of the cabinet of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and the authorised official of the military archives. And I think that you can see this from the document itself here. I told you before the break, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Radoicic, you've answered the question I think. If Mr. Hannis wants more information, he'll ask for it. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, then, so in the actual process of the physical handover at the archives someone from your office from the cabinet of the chief would have been present during the process when it was being checked by the person receiving these materials at the archive. Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is compulsory, otherwise the handover could not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we've seen on this document that the typewritten entries with the number of documents and the number of pages for each separate item, we've seen instances where there have been handwritten changes. Now, when and where would those have been made? Was that at the archives during the handover process when each document is being looked at one by one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: In the technology involved as far as I knew, and I think that I managed to deal with all of that because I was responsible and I had to ascertain all of this, when this came back, that is to say the responsible person at the cabinet of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, I did not see that these corrections were there. However, I know that the responsible person from the military archives, when receiving documentation, could either receive this documentation or refuse to receive this documentation. Or if it would happen, perhaps there were one or two cases, that it was incomplete with a certain degree of confidence he could agree to have the documentation supplemented at a later date; otherwise he would not sign that, or rather, he would not sign that he received such documents and with such numbers. This is the first time I see these corrections. Probably there is some reason in some -- on some occasion, I don't know when, I cannot say whether it was during the handover, probably it -- this correction was entered and it was initialled. And as I said to you when you showed me this page, 2, yes, yes, it is the list on page 2 where you can see the signature of that person from the military archives, then that is the responsibility of that person to receive it in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to pages 2 and 3 of the B/C/S and put them up side by side for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel, and I think we determined that the signature on the right-hand -- far right-hand column of the last page appears to be that of warrant officer first class Dusan Mladenovski?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I can just make an assumption, like you. I do not appear as an expert. I did not have occasion to see the signature of this person, but in terms of what we see here and the signature we see here, it is not my signature and it is not the signature of anyone from the office of the Chief of General Staff. So as for how meritorious all of this is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: The corrections -- the handwritten corrections that are made sometimes in the -- in column 4, which has the log number and date of the documents, and sometimes in columns 5 and 6, which list the number of documents or the number of pages, those changes, would they have been made by someone from your office or by the archivist receiving the documents, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: The only person who had the right to carry out corrections was the responsible person from the military archives. Our corrections would not be accepted. Our list had to be made very precisely, very pedantically, so that it could be prepared for handover. With such corrections -- well, that was one's attitude towards this kind of responsible job. One would not dare to go to start the procedure of handover with such corrections, let alone to have it completed that way. So the procedure had to be very precise, correct, and also it had to be very legible without a single correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This archive list, do you know how many copies of it would have been made and how they would have been distributed? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: I just know that one copy had to be, if I can put it that way, with the party that was delivering the document and another copy with the party that was receiving the document. I don't know whether the receiving party needed to have it copied further. We as the handing-over party needed just one copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So the copy you got back --

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: -- that was the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You got the original back or did the archives keep the original or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: The list itself was made in two copies, and these two copies were equal to the original. So it was a second original, it was not a carbon copy, so we cannot say that it was the second carbon copy. The other copy had to be identical to the first one, so both copies; that is to say for the receiving party and for the handing-over copy, they had to be identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you're talking about what I would refer to as duplicate originals, two copies of the same thing both intended to be treated as originals, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so in this situation where we have handwritten changes made on the document, you're saying there would be a second document with those same handwritten changes made on it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: That's the way it should be. When I say "should be," I can clarify, if necessary. I don't want to be more extensive than necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm running over my time so I'm going to try to finish quickly. Could you explain why you mean -- should be, do you mean that's the way it should be but you don't know if that happened in this particular instance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: If the corrections were made in the proper way, and judging by the signature, that's what's probably happened, then both the first duplicate original and the other duplicate original had to have been corrected in the same manner. If that was not the case, then the whole procedure was improper, but I cannot now tell you more.
