Only the officials who actually did that would be in a position to tell you more if they were, in fact, in charge of that, if that was their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the copy, the duplicate original that you as the sending party of these materials would have gotten, where would that be kept in your office, basically your receipt, I would call it, where would that be kept in your office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, you used the right term, "receipt." By signing this, you confirm that you took receipt of those documents. After the handover procedure was over, that list was supposed to be kept in metal boxes, in metal filing cabinets, in the premises of the office -- of the head of the office of the cabinet of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff or the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Colonel, do you know, could you help us out if today we wanted to go to Belgrade and try to find your office's copy of this document, where would we look for it? Where in the archives would we have to ask? What description would we give so that the Serbian authorities could help us find it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, if I were now to locate this document for you, the first thing I would do, I would go to the military archives. In the premises of the military archive, you submit a request and in this request you specify the document that you're looking for. You put in a brief written explanation, and the authorised official, the head of the military archives then deems whether this request is justified or not. If it is justified, then he meets the request in the proper manner. He shows me the document for me to see whether this is the document in question. If I am authorised to take receipt of this document for some further action, for a time-period that may be limited or not, I would then go with this document to the office of the chief of the cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff, and I would ask them to tell me what happened with this document, whether this document was retained. It would depend on the instruction that existed in the Army of Yugoslavia that envisaged to the greatest detail how documents are to be treated. It is a book that specifies how documents are to be treated, official documents, internal documents, state secret, and so on. If this list was to be kept in this metal filing cabinet permanently, then this document is supposed to be there, and if the authorised officer in charge of an organizational unit, the chef de cabinet or the Chief of General Staff, indeed, deemed that this document is to be kept permanently, then that is what it was done. But the retention time was set, one year, five years, ten years, and if this time-period has not expired, the document is there. And then with the document and the document that was taken out from the military archives, then you can simply compare the two, to see whether the -- both copies are identical. I think that I was quite ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I had phrased my question a certain way because I have some familiarity with the process because over the years we've been on several occasions trying to obtain documents from the archives. And sometimes our problem from the view of the archivist seems to be that we aren't describing the document correctly or accurately enough for them to be able to find it, and I was just wondering if you could help us with what language we should use to describe this particular document, meaning your copy that you would have gotten back after these materials were delivered to the archive. So should we make reference to the office of the chef de cabinet of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I could think of that a bit more for the following reason. Every organizational unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You're carrying out your investigation process here, Mr. Hannis. You've already had an answer that says the copy would be in the office of the chef de cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff, depending on what the arrangements were for keeping it. I imagine there's not an unending circle whereby that document would also be trailed along to the archives and a receipt received for it. But if there is, I don't think you're going to get clarification here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll stop now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder if we could have back on the screen 3D1078. Can I have it on the right-hand screen, please, on the LiveNote screen so I can magnify it on this screen. And the next page. That page in B/C/S also, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Radoicic, could you go to the second-last paragraph that you see now on the screen where Mr. Ojdanic talks about you being self-conceited and having a high opinion of your grandure. And if you go to the sixth-last paragraph, which means going back to I think the previous page unless you scroll down and we can see it - yeah, it's on this page - where he refers to it being hypocritical to refer to the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. That led to Mr. Visnjic suggesting to you in his initial questioning that you and Mr. Ojdanic were not on the best of terms. What caused him to refer to you in this way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you now with full responsibility and with full sincerity vis-a-vis Mr. Ojdanic that in this procedure the level of responsibility for the speed of my action was not sufficiently determined, and I think that I should apologise now because my powers of assessment were far less than those that he had, his assessment was broader, but on the other hand for formal and legal reasons I was prevented, I was hindered. I could not start searching for this document because pursuant to this decision of the Supreme Defence Council that I cannot now refer to precisely, but I do know that this decision prohibited the use of documents - I think that I did not add that at the beginning - documents that were classified as strictly confidential, state secret, and so on. Except in those cases where approval was obtained. At that time I was at the cabinet of the defence minister and I did not get, I did not ask, for that approval. And that is where I made this big mistake. And this is what I am responsible for. I did not ask officially for the approval to go and look for this document. And thirdly, this document was no longer within my purview because at that time it was already either at the military archives or at the cabinet of the Chief of General Staff. If you allow me, let me just finish. So the military archives in that period of time were under the administration for the information of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and I had no right to issue any orders asking to get this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What changed then after you received the letter which is now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean. Nothing changed. I got the official -- I got an official letter from him, from army General Dragoljub Ojdanic, and I replied to that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you saying his original request wasn't official?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: In that period, procedure on those requests was not something that was regulated as far as I was concerned. I was not under any obligation to do that, but I had to treat his initial request with a much higher degree of responsibility than I did, and I feel that I'm personally responsible in this case. And this is how he painted this failure on my part, and he was fully right. Whether this was my conceit, my delusion of grandure, this is not something that I manifested because my personal and my professional treatment of General Ojdanic was always the same. But at that time I was not at the level. And if you can say that I have moral responsibility for not being up to scratch, then I admit that it is the case. In the time that passed, I came to be convinced that the least that I can be charged with is moral responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When the question was originally put to you by Mr. Visnjic your answer was: "There was not a quality communication." What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN RADOICIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time when this correspondence occurred, I think that the relations between -- the relations were not regulated in a proper manner, or rather, the relations were in accordance with the regulations, but in light of the situation and in light of the needs, I think that this level of regulation was such that it did not allow me to evince a greater degree of responsibility such as I should have. The chef de cabinet of the federal defence minister did not -- was not superior to the Chief of General Staff, which was at that time fully autonomous, that is different to the current situation where the defence minister is in some aspects superior to the Chief of General Staff. It was not so at the time, and I couldn't evince this higher degree of responsibility, and that is why I considered that I did not deal with this in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Radoicic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming here to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm reminded that I should have made it clear at the outset today that Judge Nosworthy's absence is on account of urgent personal business and that we did consider the position again this morning and decided to continue in her absence in the interests of justice. Your next witness, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our next witness is General Milan Uzelac. Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness I can tell you that this will be a viva voce witness and we anticipated his testimony would take about 20 minutes, and it will mostly be about parts of evidence of witness Djorovic, Prosecution witness Lakic Djorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Uzelac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General.

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you please tell the Trial Chamber briefly about your military career, which duties you performed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: I began my career just like the majority of officers in the units of the Army of Yugoslavia. The last three functions that I carried out in the General Staff were the independent desk officer, expert desk officer, for analysis or planning of movement; deputy chief of the transport administration; and then the chief of the transport administration until the end of my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, which duties were you performing in the course of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: In the course of 1999, I was the chief of the administration -- transport administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the second half of 1999, was the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia resolving the problem of vehicles that were in the possession of the Army of Yugoslavia and were not from the establishment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what it means when the vehicles are not from the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: When the vehicles are not from the establishment, it means that they are not entered in the military central register and that they come from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please look at the table Exhibit P2752, this is a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you are aware of this document and the document is titled: "Overview of confiscated and seized motor vehicles."

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: The document was drafted by the transport administration in the second half of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In terms of structure, General, where did these vehicles come from, General? And before that let me ask you what was the purpose of this overview?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: The overview was drafted in order to resolve the issue of vehicles that were in the units of the army and were not in the establishment structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And now you can tell me, we have a table here where it is clearly stated where -- which units the vehicles are from, the type or model of the vehicles, their number. Where did these vehicles come from, how did they end up in the units of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: The precise answer how individual vehicles ended up in the units is something that we are not able to answer. We were not able to give an answer to that at that time either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But do you have a broader idea, a broader picture?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes. According to information, the vehicles came from customs, where they were seized and given to the army for temporary use. A certain number of vehicles were given from -- by the judiciary organs which had been seized during the commission of crimes, and a number came from the areas where combat activities were carried out. There is a certain number of vehicles among the total number that were mobilised but were not returned in time because the addresses of those who had provided them were unknown and did not have the required documents that are necessary in order to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: For purposes of the transcript, page 55, line 2, you said that a number of vehicles were given to the army by customs. Am I correct? Did I hear you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's line 49 [sic] of page 54. Customs, judiciary, and combat areas are the three sources that he's given.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say here that a number of the vehicles was mobilised. How did you come to that conclusion? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: The conclusion comes from the number of freight vehicles and buses, and the figure given for those vehicles here is a total of 450.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The expression "mobilised but were not returned in time," what do you mean by "in time"? Do you simply mean after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And now, General, do you have some rough idea perhaps of how many of the vehicles out of the total number or in percentages came from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and how many came from other sources that you mentioned a little bit earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: In my rough estimate and according to my best recollection, it would be from 60 to 65 per cent of vehicles that came from Kosovo and Metohija and the others were from other areas or from customs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, we said here before that the General Staff was trying to resolve the issue of these vehicles. What was the problem that you actually had with these vehicles? Can you please explain that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: The problem of these vehicles the General Staff began to deal with right after the beginning of the war when these vehicles remained in the units and were not returned to their owners, the resolution of the problem was something that was initiated by the units because they needed to be removed from the units as soon as possible because they were creating costs, there was a problem of how to maintain them and protect them from being taken away or spare parts being taken away. So also there was the problem of the engagement of the units on a daily basis on their maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the second half of 1999, were there any meetings held in order to resolve that problem and can you please explain the procedure that was adopted in order to resolve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: In the beginning the problem was supposed to be resolved at the level of the expert service transport administration at whose head -- which I headed later. Then we had some problems relating to the legal nature of this matter and we asked the legal structures from the army and the ministry to assist us to find a legal solution in order to resolve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I see that you said that you tried to resolve this at the level of your service, the transport administration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How did you try to resolve this problem, what was the initial position, what was the initial proposal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: The initial proposal was to settle this in the way that vehicles after being used in the army which are not part of the army are actually returned to the owners, and this procedure is very precisely laid down. And according to the procedure, vehicles returned from -- are returned to known owners and there would be a commission report made as well as accompanying documents in the process. These vehicles did not have proper documents, and then there was the problem of how to return the vehicles in their original state.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you said that for that purpose you sought the opinion of specific legal services?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it this problem relates to the ones which were taken in areas of combat, that the problem doesn't relate to customs or the judiciary as sources of these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem had to do with all the vehicles mentioned here regardless of whether they came from areas where there was combat or whether they came from customs, for the simple reason that anything used in the army, any item, has to have the appropriate documents regulating the use of that item. The vehicles in question did not have proper documents because they were issued for use with decisions. And then there was a problem for all the vehicles to find a uniform solution and to adjust that to the needs. This was the reason why the -- some of the vehicles in question were received from customs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you said one thing. You said that the vehicles from customs were issued with documents that were actually just for temporary use, and I see that is not in the transcript, the documents were for the temporary use. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it is in the transcript. Was there a problem then with the documents relating to vehicles which came from courts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vehicles that came from the courts that -- did not present a problem because there was the proper procedure. When a decision is made during proceedings that a vehicle is being seized or confiscated, that was used in the commission of a crime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question I asked you. Please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us something about meetings that were held in order to resolve this matter, when these meetings were held, who attended them, and ultimately what was the final result of such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: The first meeting after the usual consultations and an attempt to get a solution at the level of legal services, a meeting was held - I cannot give the exact date - sometime in July or August of 1999 which was attended by invited representatives of the legal administration of the ministry, the General Staff, the security service, these were all legal experts, and there were also people from the judiciary, representatives of the court attended the meetings, and of course expert organs of the transport administration in an attempt to find a joint solution and to receive expert assistance in the resolution of this problem. At that meeting the opinion prevailed that this was regulated in the regulations, transport organs were of the view that this procedure was quite slow and that this was not the best solution, at least in our opinion. However, as the discussion continued, the conclusion was reached that there was no other way other than to go through the regular procedure which was valid at that time, it's probably still valid now, for all items that are in that particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: A person called Dasic, did that person chair any one of those meetings and do you know who that might be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: I chaired the meeting that I referred to. As for a person by the name of Dasic, at that time this person did not work at the General Staff and therefore could not attend such a meeting, let alone chair such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Otherwise you know who Dasic is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's a general who came to work at the General Staff, as far as I can remember, towards the end of 2002. All of this was happening in the second half of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did General Ojdanic ever bring any pressure to bear upon you for having this resolved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether General Ojdanic exerted pressure upon any one of your associates or persons who participated in these meetings in order to have this question resolved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did General Ojdanic directly or indirectly communicate with you in order to try to resolve this matter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: General Ojdanic did not communicate with me, either directly or indirectly, because he was my second superior officer. One's assignments are received from one's immediate superior officer and over those years I did not receive any assignments directly from the Chief of General Staff, not only in relation to this but generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was there any mention at any one of these meetings that Ojdanic and Pavkovic were furious because the vehicles had not been allocated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: No. These meetings, these two meetings that were organized, the first one that I spoke about and the second one that was attended by a larger number of people and where this table was presented at a later point. There was no reference to that, especially because General Pavkovic at that time was not in the General Staff at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a table now, General. This table was compiled by you, or rather, your service, not Generals Gojkovic and Obrencevic; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. This table could not have been compiled by anyone but the professional organs because they have all the records of vehicles, both those that are in the central register and those that were not in that register.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, who was your direct superior, the one that was between you and General Ojdanic in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: The person who was assistant Chief of General Staff, that was Lieutenant-Colonel-General Vidoje Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in your position as chief of the transport administration, what -- what is that exactly? What was your job in 1999? Can you briefly describe your duties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: In the General Staff every administration has its precisely prescribed powers and responsibilities in terms of military establishment. As for the transportation administration, it was in charge of planning movement, training personnel for the transport service; that is to say drivers and others, and obtaining motor vehicles and registering them. Those are the basic, most important tasks that were there, also regulating the safety of traffic, may I add that too, that is the most important work that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately how many people worked under you? How many people worked in the transportation administration of the VJ in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was between 13 and 14 persons, engineers who worked in this administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With the onset of the NATO bombing, was there a change in your duties or did they remain basically the same?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: The duties remained basically the same, except that during the bombing two or three other men were brought in to help because we worked round the clock, 24 hours a day, so it was necessary in order to be able to take it physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned that the problem with these vehicles that we were talking about is that they were not entered in the military central register. Can you explain for me, please, what is the military central register?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: In the army there is a central register where every vehicle that is in the possession of the army is registered, and one knows exactly in what unit it is, when it was manufactured, and everything else that is required. Vehicles that were obtained in three ways can become part of this central register and that have full and regular documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What are those three ways?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: First way is buying from the market or from the manufacturer, where contracts are made, payments are made, and the vehicle is brought into the records. The second way is that when judiciary organs complete a procedure and seize a vehicle in accordance with regulations, then the transportation administration is the tactical mainstay to which this is reported and then they allocate the vehicle as necessary. And thirdly, the third possible way is if a physical person or a legal person wishes to make a gift to the military, then appropriate documentation is drafted and that is how a vehicle is received. That is how all the vehicles were obtained, all of those that are in the central register of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For vehicles that were obtained either through a gift, as you just described, or that came as a result of a judicial forfeiture proceeding of some sort, who decided where those vehicles would be allocated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Such a decision as well as for vehicles that are obtained in the other two ways is made by the transportation administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What happens to vehicle -- or about vehicles which are requisitioned during wartime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these are the vehicles that we have been describing so far. They were supposed to be returned to their previous owners. They were supposed to go through a certain procedure and to be returned to those who owned them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The word "requisition" means seized, if necessary, against the will of the owner. Such vehicles would not appear to fall into any of the three categories you've given us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of these vehicles that are portrayed in this table do not belong to those three categories. That is the source of the problem that we tried to resolve during the course of 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So requisitioned for the use of the army for military purposes, say during the state of war, that's a fourth way that the VJ might physically obtain vehicles, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: This concept of requisitioning is not something that we had, as far as I know. I mean, I don't know how to explain this now, but this requisitioning was never used as a concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I thought we had had some evidence earlier in this case that there was a process whereby during wartime the army, for necessary purposes, for military purposes, could requisition vehicles from private citizens or from private companies. Wasn't there such a process in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: That was supposed to be called mobilised vehicles that are given along with a certificate, and you know who gives it and then a compensation is provided, too, as well as for vehicles that were on lists before the war started, on lists of units, for use in the case of war or some other necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, General. It may be a language thing. I think we're talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we may be, but they would not appear in the register?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question. I'm not quite sure that I understood it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These questions that Mr. Hannis is asking are about the -- what you described as the military central register, and you've told us the three categories of vehicle which do go into the register. Can we take it that those which are mobilised vehicles do not go into the register?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The evidence I was thinking of, General, actually came from Colonel Pesic, who testified on the 23rd of November last year. And at page 7222, line 5, now he's talking about the military district, but I'm curious as to whether or not the same procedure doesn't apply to the VJ. He said that during a state of war there was authorisation to requisition or appropriate civilian vehicles or private properties. He said: "It's a planned activity to provide sufficient number of vehicles for the units. That planned activity is implemented by military sectors in order to meet the needs," in this case of the Pristina Corps, "and the needs of the military territorial detachments." Were you familiar with that procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not called requisitioning, at least not in our terminology, and it does not mean violent seizing of vehicles. It means that military territorial organs that are in charge of providing the required number of vehicles can, along with a certificate, take an additional number of vehicles that before the war, or rather, in preparation for carrying out tasks had not been earmarked for use by the military. I have to point out here that these vehicles that are mobilised involve a certain procedure. Every year they are checked by a commission and their owners know that, if necessary, they should bring their vehicles in to a particular place and a record is made. One knows when the vehicle was brought in and what the payments made would be for every day that was used by the military, so that is unequivocal. However, if vehicles were destroyed during the bombing or if there was a need for increasing capacities, it is possible to do something additional about this, but again a certificate has to be issued and these vehicles are treated the same way as those other vehicles, except that there is not a record that is compiled by the commission. Quite simply, a certificate is issued, and then on the basis of that all the rights are regulated. I think that it is the word "requisitioning" that caused this confusion. No one requisitioned vehicles, at least not legally, the military territorial organs did not do that, they did not take vehicles in that way and they did not evade making the payments that were due to the owners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I didn't mean to suggest that they were, General. But that seems to be now a fifth way that the army might obtain vehicles, and the vehicles that were obtained by the military territorial organs under this procedure that Colonel Pesic described, would those have been entered in the central register of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: No. Let me clarify once again. As for the central register, it lists only vehicles that are owned by the military. They don't have to pay any compensation for that and they don't have to return these vehicles to anyone. These are vehicles that are in the permanent possession of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I don't have a group four and five I don't think. My impression is that all of this is about the same methodology of acquiring vehicles which the witness describes as mobilised vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I guess I saw a distinction between what Colonel Pesic has described with the military district sort of pre-planning the need for vehicles and having a list of vehicles to be mobilised when needed, as opposed to sort of the ad hoc what I would call requisition of vehicles, for example, during or after the onset of combat by military units in the field and requisitioning civilian vehicles from people on the spot, which we've had some testimony about. I think Mr. Bucaliu who talked about that in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that you can divine more than four categories from all the evidence, but I wonder if this witness is describing five categories. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As long as you understand the distinction I was trying to draw, Your Honour, that's all I need to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, you mentioned -- I mean General, sorry, you mentioned that one of the problems or concerns you had about these vehicles in late 1999 was how to protect them from being taken away or parts being taken away from them. From whom did the army have to protect these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: During the air-strikes, I have to tell you now, more -- many of the barracks, the garrisons, and the hangars --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm talking about after the war. I understood you had been talking about in late 1999, after July 1999; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So after July 1999, who were you trying to protect these vehicles from being taken away?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Well, I tried to explain that. The vehicles were in their units. The vehicles were not all gathered in one place, they were in their units. And because during the air-strikes the barracks had been destroyed, defences had been destroyed and the enclosed areas where those vehicles could be kept in a safe manner were also destroyed both from the weather and theft. This was protected against civilians, all kinds of thieves that could get into those areas that had not been repaired yet, and definitely this was a potential risk. There was this risk of theft, and that is why I mentioned that this problem had to be resolved and to have those vehicles returned to their vehicles [as interpreted] as soon as possible. We were not supposed to keep them for such a long time in the units and in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned meetings that you attended in late 1999 to talk about this problem with these vehicles that weren't listed in the central register. I think you said there were two meetings. Is that the total number of meetings you remember attending to discuss this issue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: I mentioned at the beginning of my evidence that at the level of the professional service there was several consultations and meetings within the transportation administration in an effort to find a solution. When we were no longer -- when we exhausted all our possibilities for solving this problem, we organized the first meeting I think with the five or six lawyers from all the legal services in the army and the ministry, and some progress was made in order to achieve a legal solution for this issue, that was based on the regulations in force and legal practice. The second meeting was organized sometime in November, and a larger number of people was invited to that meeting, and the seriousness of this whole problem was discussed and possible costs for the army unless this problem is resolved was also discussed. There were representatives of the ministry, of the General Staff, and primarily from the legal and transport service, transportation service, they were present there. So those were the two main meetings where these issues were addressed. There were no other meetings of this nature because the position was taken at those meetings as to how this should be resolved within the legal framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You described those as the two main meetings. Can you tell us approximately when the first one was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Well, I can't now recall the exact date, but I think it was sometime in late July or early August of that year, 1999, and the second meeting was sometime in November of the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall where each of those meetings were, the first one in July or August?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. The first meeting was in my office and I chaired the meeting, and the second meeting was held in the -- in a hall in the General Staff building and it was attended by substantially larger number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many people attended that second meeting in November?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Well, between 25 and 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the first meeting in your office, how many at that one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Well, there may have been seven or eight people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Obrencevic attend either of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: No. I don't know for the second one, but he did not attend the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Finally I want to ask you about Exhibit P2572 which is this table of confiscated and seized motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we put that on the e-court for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, is that the table that was being referred to at the very end of the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the document that's now in front of us, the war log?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes -- no, sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I gave the wrong information. It should be 2752, I think I transposed my digits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At the end of your examination-in-chief you asked the witness if a table was compiled and he said it was compiled by his staff. Is that the same as the document you had put on the screen, which is P2752?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, is this the document that was prepared by your transportation administration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was this used in connection with that November meeting? I see the date on it is the 23rd of November, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: I presented this overview because I also took part in that meeting in an effort to find a solution and I took part in the debate. This overview was presented at that meeting, and it was made quite some time before because we knew what problem we were supposed to deal with and we knew about the number of vehicles we had to have some foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it none of these vehicles, these 1.913 total are vehicles that were purchased or were the subject of judicial forfeitures or gifts to the army. These are all vehicles that were not in the central register, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the 1.333 listed in connection with the 3rd Army in the third row there, how many of those, if you know, came to the army during combat activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: A long time has passed since then. I could not really give you a definite answer, because even before 1999 we would get vehicles from the customs for temporary use and they were then assigned to units. At this point in time I don't have the exact figures for the number of such vehicles that reached the 3rd Army before the bombing started so I really couldn't give you any reliable information as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you can't tell us out of this number, 1.333, how many came to the army before the bombing started and how many came after?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you because a long time has passed, but I know that quite a few vehicles had come from the customs in 1997 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So how long had these 1.333 vehicles been in the possession of the army without being returned or without being listed on the central register? Is this a problem that's been going back for a couple of years before 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I understand your question correctly. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'll withdraw it and ask you something else. Was there detailed information kept somewhere in the army or in the transportation administration about the sources of each of these 1.333 vehicles, or did that simply not exist?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: We did not have such unified records. We only kept records as to the number and kind of vehicles in each unit, and on the basis of the reports from the units we were able to produce this overview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It seems -- it seems likely to me that a certain number of these vehicles must have been seized from private individuals and companies in Kosovo during 1998 and 1999. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after the end of the war, after June 1999, what efforts did you, the transportation administration in the army, make to try and identify the rightful owners and return the vehicles to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: The transportation administration and the General Staff made efforts immediately after the end of the war to have those vehicles returned to their owners as soon as possible, but in that period it was quite difficult for a very simple reason. It was, in fact, impossible to locate all the owners simply because many people from Kosovo had left, had come to Serbia, to central Serbia, or went abroad, changed their addresses, and we didn't know where they were. Secondly, as regards the population or Kosovo and Metohija, the communication or the possibility to reach the legal owners were low and it was difficult to do so, and for some vehicles the owners were not known. The owners were supposed to report themselves, they were supposed to file a request for their vehicle to be returned to them. Some efforts were made, in other words, but it was quite obvious that at that time it was not such a simple -- not such an easy task, and that is why this meeting was set up in order to see ways in which this could be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we're well past the time for the break. Have you got a lot to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did or the army make any efforts to make a public notification calling upon owners of vehicles that had been taken by the army to come forward and identify themselves and provide information about their vehicles? You didn't do that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: We didn't make any such public calls, but there were some owners who knew, owners knew that they could seek their vehicles, the return of their vehicles, through legal offices or in some other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you just told us that the owners came. My question to you is whether you know that even after those meetings the owners from Kosovo and Metohija had their vehicles returned to them.

utterances.speaker: MILAN UZELAC
utterances.text: The owners who had documents, who had proof of the ownership of the vehicles, the vehicles were returned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Uzelac, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom. Mr. Visnjic, remind me of the estimate for Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the fact that it's Friday, I'll do my best to complete his evidence within 15 to 20 minutes max. He's testifying under Rule 92 bis, so there will be just some quick additional examination -- 92 ter, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm -- simply ask because there is the potential of -- we're not under the extreme pressure of finishing exactly at quarter to. So I think we should do our level best together to complete his evidence today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- well, the very fact that it's Friday today is pressure enough, but we will do all we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall adjourn now and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it happens to each team in turn, Mr. Visnjic, so Mr. Ackerman will be next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic is going to blame me for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please give us your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: My name is Vidoje Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Before you start your testimony, I wish to ask you whether it is correct that on the 16th of September, 2007, you gave a statement to the Defence team of General Ojdanic and that you signed it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that during the proofing for your testimony here you had a look at this statement?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: As for the questions that were put to you while your statement was being taken, would you give the same answers if you were to testify live before this court?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, tell us what were the duties that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before we --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. [Interpretation] 3D1113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell me what duties you had in 1998.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1998 I was chief of the operative logistics administration in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and at the same time I was deputy assistant Chief of General Staff for logistics. And in 1999 from the 18th of January, or rather, on the 18th of January I became chief -- assistant Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I continue the examination of this witness, I wish to inform you that we intend to tender the following documents: 3D1075, that is the collegium on the 12th of December, 1997, that is referred to in paragraphs 5 and 6 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to go into any detail regarding this document. We can give the exact references in writing what paragraphs of this document we are relying upon, if that is convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be very helpful, Mr. Visnjic, if you were to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we'll admit it subject to clarification of the paragraphs that you -- the parts of it that you rely upon. Can we expect that to be done before the end of next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're probably going to do that already today. We'll send an e-mail and probably we will submit this on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll mark it for identification until we see your e-mail. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Also documents 3D743, 3D744, 3D745, and 3D746. These documents are relevant for paragraphs 30, 31, and 32 of the witness's statement, and it has to do with the relationship between the MUP and the Army of Yugoslavia in terms of logistics. With the witness I just want to go through two more documents here live. Could the witness please be shown 3D1097.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're referring to these other four exhibits on the basis that the witness doesn't say in his statement he's been shown these and say anything about them, but you say that they're relevant to the issues which arise in paragraphs 30, 31, and 32?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. He does not rely on them, but it is obvious from the documents that they actually confirm what the witness is testifying about. These are very brief documents, they are not too extensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see no objection being taken to you presenting them in this way so these will be admitted -- oh, sorry, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I didn't know he was asking for them to be admitted. I heard him telling the Court what they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The policy has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're opposing this, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the documents have not been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't know what they are?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I see the documents here and I can go on the face of them but I think the documents should be identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you objecting to them being admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No foundation has been laid as to what they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid you're going to have to go through them, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Then let's show the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your alternative is to make a bar table filing, but this may be quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept the alternative, Your Honour, and in our request we are going to say exactly what the paragraphs are that the witness is referring to. Could the witness please be shown 3D1097.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us what kind of a document this is, when it was created?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is an order of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia for a tour and control of commands and units in the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps. It was created on the 2nd of March, 1999, and the tour was planned for the 3rd and 4th of March the same year. This order defines the tasks that the control, or rather, the tour would involve in the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. As far as I can see here from paragraph 2 of this order, this group shall headed by General Ojdanic personally, Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. General Dragoljub Ojdanic personally headed this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell us who was on the control group, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: As for the control group, there were a few of us there, his immediate assistant chiefs; in addition to General Ojdanic there was the chief of sector of operations and staff affairs, General Obradovic; then there was me; then from security I think it was General Gajic. I cannot recall all the names right now that were ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, if I understand you correctly, you were there?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How many days did this take?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: This tour took two days, the 3rd and 4th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document 1098, 3D1098.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what does this document represent?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: This document is a plan for touring commands and units in the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps of the 3rd Army. For every task that is planned, a plan is made and one acts within a given period of time in accordance with the plan made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 3, please, in B/C/S and page 2 in English, please, or rather, page 3, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, General, it is my understanding that this activity, or rather, this trip was planned in detail.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, in detail from the departure from the General Staff to the arrival at the airport, and then from Batajnica airport we flew to Zlatan airport in Pristina --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, General, you don't have to go into all this detail. The Judges can read this for themselves. What I wanted to ask you is the following: To the best of your recollection throughout this two-day activity were you with General Ojdanic all the time?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, I was with him all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: From this itinerary here --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, it is on pages 3, 4, and 5 in B/C/S, I assume that it's similar in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- you had many intensive meetings in various units, and also - I see that here from a particular column - you had a meeting with the organs of local government and the state authorities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as for all of these meetings involving the military and the civilian authorities and the units that you toured, were there any discussions at any one of these meetings concerning expulsions of the Albanian population from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, not at a single meeting, including during this tour, was there any such discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were there any discussions about any activities that could resemble population movements, movements of the civilian population from Kosovo, from one territory to another or -- or having them transferred across the border?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, there were no such discussions. There were no such plans. As a matter of fact, we flew by helicopter, we took a car, we took cars in the territory. The population was involved in its normal spring activities, agricultural activities, and from the helicopters you could see their houses and their yards and their fields. And there was no indication whatsoever of that nature, no mention of any such thing in discussions with the authorities, nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I start by indicating that I withdraw the objection in respect to 3D743 to 746. I don't think it's necessary to file the paperwork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Thank you. So we'll regard these as admitted in conjunction with the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You maintained high-level contacts with the minister of interior, particularly Mr. Stojiljkovic, in respect to the delivery of armaments and ammunition to the MUP for MUP activities, didn't you? And when I say "you," I mean the command of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. To the best of my knowledge, the command of the army, or rather, the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia or the Supreme Command Staff during the course of the war did not hold any special links, did not have any special links with Minister Stojiljkovic, minister of the interior. As for this subject which is of interest, generally speaking when the MUP needed something they would address the Army of Yugoslavia in the prescribed way, in writing, through a written document that would be signed by Minister Stojiljkovic and that the army would examine. And within the scope of its possibilities, it would meet their needs or could not. Minister Stojiljkovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the answer. Could all microphones please be switched off except for the speaker's. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you could repeat the end of your answer there since the interpreter was unable to pick it up. You were saying: "And within the scope of its possibilities," that's the VJ, "it would meet their needs or could not." You said: "Minister Stojiljkovic," and the rest was lost.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Minister Stojiljkovic did not appear in person or in some other way, except that he signed documents that would come in written form to the General Staff or, possibly, to the Federal Ministry of Defence and then that would be forwarded to the General Staff for having it ultimately resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could look quickly at P1910, if that could be brought up on e-court. And if we could move to page 2 in the English and remain on the -- on page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 6, in the middle of paragraph 6, sir, you will see an indication of arrangements being made for take-over of equipment from the Army of the Republika Srpska. Do you see that? Are you able to read that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were -- were your supplies of armoured vehicles and tanks augmented by supplies from Republika Srpska in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. Not a single tank was received from the Army of Republika Srpska. It is clear here, stated here, that the overhaul institution, the technical facility in the Army of Yugoslavia that overhauled some of the equipment of Republika Srpska, agreement was received that some of the equipment that was being overhauled could be given to the Army of Yugoslavia for its use. We always said what it was. It was some types of infantry weapons, motors for the T-55 tank, I don't know exactly how many tank engines were involved, but it certainly could not have been more. Then one power generator and 537G, that's it. There were no tanks that the Army of Yugoslavia got from the Army of Republika Srpska or from anyone else in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you don't know of any tank units or tank formations being transferred from Republika Srpska to the VJ in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. I can say with full certainty that there weren't any such situations. There were no tank units from the Army of Republika Srpska that would come to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we now move to your statement at paragraphs 13 and 14 and 15. Do you have it there, your statement, paragraphs 13 and 14?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll just read it to you then. Paragraph 13 says that: "The VJ was financed from the FRY budget. The 1999 budget did not contain any increase in the funds for the event of a war so that the whole 1999 war was financed from the peacetime budget adopted by the federal government in December 1999." Paragraph 14 says: "The VJ budget was about 10 million dinars, but due to the outstanding payments from 1999 amounting to about 2 billion dinars, it was actually lower for this amount. Moreover, the budget did not contain any funds in foreign currency for equipping the army with imported goods." The part I wish to focus on is the budget did not contain any funds in foreign currency for equipping the army with foreign goods. Were there international sanctions against Yugoslavia which prevented it from importing weaponry for the VJ or some types of weaponry for the VJ? And I should give you a date. Were these sanctions in place in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all I would like to correct you. We're not talking about 10 million, we're talking about 10 billion dinars. At that time the equivalent would be about $1 billion. It is correct that at that time sanctions were in place. We did not have any foreign currency to import anything from abroad, and we couldn't import anything because the wall of the sanctions was really very firm. So the import of any materiel or anything from abroad into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia during the war was completely impossible, and we were very desperately short of some items at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know that during the time when these sanctions were in place a financial structure was designed and implemented by President Milosevic for the funding, equipping, and supplying of the VJ by diverting funds from customs duties that were collected to foreign bank accounts and to foreign arms suppliers, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. Nobody's ever told me about that and there was no discussion of that. I didn't know what kind of items were supposed to be obtained in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You were assistant chief for logistics, so I'll ask you this then. Do you know that the VJ was supplied with helicopter -- helicopter parts and high technology spare parts from abroad through sums of money diverted by Slobodan Milosevic to foreign bank accounts for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like Mr. Stamp to show some foundation for these questions. I let him ask the first one, but now I would really like him to give us some kind of a foundation where does this come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm merely asking the witness if he knows these things, but if it is necessary and if it is helpful, these are the results -- or these are the findings of -- in an expert report that was used in the Milosevic case and that was disclosed to the Defence a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does Mr. Stamp mean that this report is among the millions of pages that were disclosed to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I wasn't sure I was expected to answer. This was disclosed to Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was among the millions of pages; if that is so, Your Honour, this was not exhibited in the proceedings so far and I would like Mr. Stamp to provide us with the foundation for the questions he's asking of the witness. Well, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The last words you uttered are translated: "It doesn't matter."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry, that was an aside that was meant for Mr. Ivetic. I apologise. And I'm still waiting for Mr. Stamp's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think it's for Mr. Stamp to answer. It's obvious that he's claiming that these were disclosed to you but not exhibited as yet in the trial. Give us one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're happy to rely on Mr. Stamp's assurance about his foundation and we'll allow the witness to answer the question. If it emerges in due course that some prejudice has been caused to you, Mr. Visnjic, then you know that you can apply to us for relief from that. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm merely asking you, sir, what you know. And am I to understand from your evidence you do not know of the VJ being supplied in 1997, 1998, and 1999 with armaments and spare parts for armaments from overseas?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: As for 1997 and 1998, I cannot give you an answer; and as for 1999, I can say with absolute certainty that there were no purchases, no spare parts, weapons, or anything was obtained from abroad in the period of time from the 18th of January when I took over until the end of the war in May -- or in June, rather. The procedure for the procurement of weapons and equipment in the Army of Yugoslavia is quite strictly regulated. It is carried out through the administration for procurement, which was at the Ministry of Defence, physically at the Ministry of Defence, and it was under the jurisdiction of the federal defence minister. The procurement could be carried out only if the assistant to the Chief of General Staff for air force and air defence in this case obtains funds, in this case that would need to be foreign exchange, dollars, pounds, marks, whatever, foreign currency of some sort. And if this assistant submits a report to the administration for procurement and then a tender goes out or the administration finds the dealer, and then the parts come in. In this period no such thing happened. I don't know anything about any such instances that you just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the period that you can speak about is the period beginning January 18th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, it was simply not possible. It was simply not possible at all. Nobody in the world --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I want Mr. Stamp to tell me, because now I remember this report quite clearly, this was disclosed to us, it comes from the Milosevic report, not because he disclosed it to us but because it was in Milosevic case. I want Mr. Stamp to tell us where he got the idea that the helicopters were actually obtained for the Army of Yugoslavia, because I don't think that that report says anything about those helicopters being bought for the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't think it's necessary for Mr. Stamp to demonstrate anything of the sort in relation to these questions. He's simply asking for this witness's knowledge of these matters. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You started out your last answer or the one before that by saying you can't speak for 1997 and 1998. What I want to understand from you is that because you were appointed to your position as chief of logistics in January 1999 ...

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the question is. I replied that there had been no imports. The Yugoslav air force did not fly at all from April on. There was no sense --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you, sir.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- for any parts to be obtained in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm asking you: Is your knowledge about the source of parts for the VJ limited to the period after you were appointed to the position of chief of logistics in January 1999?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand now. No, no. I'm absolutely certain about what I say for the previous period, too. I was the assistant Chief of General Staff for logistics, but the air force technical service was not part of the logistics sector --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That was not my question.

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- it was subordinated to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further to ask this witness. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P1910.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last paragraph on page 1, General, Mr. Stamp put it to you that some tanks or whatever it may be on this list were actually taken over from the Republika Srpska army. It says here that equipment and materiel was overhauled that was offered by the Cacak Repairs Institute. Could you please tell us what Cacak TRZ is?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: The Cacak Technical Repairs Institute is a place where the highest level of repairs were carried out in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, just one more question. Where is Cacak?

utterances.speaker: VIDOJE PANTELIC
utterances.text: Cacak is 150 kilometres away from Belgrade in Serbia, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm waiting for you to ask me if we have any further witnesses for the rest of today so that I can tell you we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're better keeping quiet. I think we resume in the afternoon on Monday, so we shall adjourn now and resume at 2.15 on Monday.
